section.title: The Wrath of God Revealed
section.sectionRationale: Having announced that the gospel reveals the righteousness of God, Paul now shows why such good news is needed: the wrath of God is being revealed against all human godlessness. He traces the deepest human sin to its root, the suppression of the truth about God that is plainly displayed in creation, and the exchange of the Creator's glory for idols. Three times he says God gave them over, handing rebels to the very desires they chose, until the passage ends in a sober catalog of a debased mind. This is the universal human problem the gospel answers.
section.thesis: The wrath of God is justly revealed against a humanity that knows God from creation yet suppresses the truth and exchanges His glory for idols; and God's righteous judgment is expressed by giving rebels over to their chosen desires, leaving all people without excuse and in desperate need of the righteousness the gospel supplies.
section.frameNote: The indictment unfolds in five movements: the wrath of God revealed against suppressed truth; the great exchange of God's glory for images; God giving them over to impurity; God giving them over to dishonorable passions; and God giving them up to a debased mind, ending in a catalog of sins that all people know deserve death.

units.label: The wrath of God revealed
units.note: God plainly known, so no one is without excuse

verses.text: The {{orge|wrath}} of God is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wickedness of men who suppress the {{aletheia|truth}} by their wickedness.
For what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them.
For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse.

units.label: The great exchange
units.note: the glory of God traded for images

verses.text: For although they knew God, they neither glorified Him as God nor gave thanks to Him, but they became futile in their thinking and darkened in their foolish hearts.
Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools,
and exchanged the {{doxa|glory}} of the immortal God for images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles.
Therefore God {{paradidomi|gave them over}} in the desires of their hearts to impurity for the dishonoring of their bodies with one another.
They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is forever worthy of praise! Amen.
For this reason God gave them over to dishonorable passions. Even their women exchanged natural relations for unnatural ones.
Likewise, the men abandoned natural relations with women and burned with lust for one another. Men committed indecent acts with other men and received in themselves the due penalty for their error.

units.label: Given up to a debased mind
units.note: the third handing over and its catalog

verses.text: Furthermore, since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, He gave them up to a {{adokimos|depraved}} mind, to do what ought not to be done.
They have become filled with every kind of wickedness, evil, greed, and depravity. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice. They are gossips,
slanderers, God-haters, insolent, arrogant, and boastful. They invent new forms of evil; they disobey their parents.
They are senseless, faithless, heartless, merciless.
Although they know God’s righteous decree that those who do such things are worthy of death, they not only continue to do these things, but also approve of those who practice them.

orge.gloss: Wrath, settled anger, the just and holy opposition of God to all evil. This is not petulant rage but the righteous response of a good God to sin, His refusal to be indifferent to the ruin of what He made. The wrath revealed here is the dark backdrop against which the righteousness of God in the gospel shines.

aletheia.gloss: Truth, reality as it actually is, especially the truth about God plainly shown in creation. Fallen humanity does not merely lack this truth but actively suppresses it, holding it down like a spring forced under water. To exchange this truth for a lie is the essence of idolatry.

doxa.gloss: Glory, weight, radiant honor; the visible splendor of God's own being. Humanity was made to reflect and enjoy this glory, but in sin traded the glory of the immortal God for images of created things. Every idol is an attempt to replace the incomparable glory of God with something smaller and manageable.

paradidomi.gloss: To hand over, deliver up, give into another's power. Three times God gives sinners over to the desires they have chosen, a judicial abandonment in which He removes His restraint and lets sin run its course. This handing over is itself a present expression of wrath, sin becoming its own punishment.

adokimos.gloss: Failing the test, unfit, disqualified, worthless. Because they refused to see God fit to acknowledge, God gave them over to a mind that is itself unfit, unable to judge rightly. There is a fitting justice in it: a mind that rejected the knowledge of God becomes a mind that no longer works as it should.

basic.context: This passage begins the long argument of Romans by establishing the universal need for the gospel. Before Paul can show how God saves, he must show why salvation is needed. He describes humanity in rebellion, not as ignorant but as knowing God through creation and then suppressing that knowledge, so that the wrath of God is justly revealed against all.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as the first half of a case that runs through Romans 3, proving that the whole world, Gentile here and Jew in chapter 2, is guilty before God. Notice the repeated words: they exchanged and God gave them over. The structure is a downward spiral, sin leading to judgment leading to more sin. It is meant to silence every mouth and drive us to grace.
basic.originalLanguages: The orge, the wrath, of God is revealed against those who suppress the aletheia, the truth. They traded the doxa, the glory, of God for idols, so God practiced paradidomi, handing them over, three times, until they were left with an adokimos, an unfit and disqualified, mind.
basic.typology: The passage recalls the fall and the golden calf: as Adam and later Israel exchanged the glory of God for a lie and an image, so all humanity repeats the pattern. The idolatry condemned here reverses creation, where humanity was made in God's image to reflect His glory rather than fashion gods in the image of creatures.
basic.christ: Christ is the answer this dark passage requires. He is the true image of God who did not suppress the truth but embodied it, the one who bore the wrath revealed here so that those given over to sin might be given a new heart. The righteousness of God in the gospel is the only rescue from the condemnation this text describes.
basic.god: This passage is God-centered even in describing sin. God is the Creator plainly revealed, the one whose glory is exchanged, the righteous Judge whose wrath is revealed, and the one who in holy justice gives rebels over. His forbearance in the present handing over still leaves the door open for the mercy of the gospel.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 3 tells the first exchange of God's word for a lie. Psalm 19 and Acts 14:17 affirm creation's witness to God. Ephesians 2:3 calls all people by nature children of wrath. Romans 3:23 sums up the verdict: all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
basic.oneStory: The Bible's story of a good creation gone wrong is compressed here. Humanity, made to know and glorify God, suppressed the truth and worshiped the creature, and God justly gave them over. This is the plight the whole of Scripture answers, the reason the gospel of Romans 1:16-17 is such good news, and the darkness against which the coming righteousness of God shines.

context.literary:
Romans 1:18 opens with the word 'for' (gar), and the connection matters. Verses 16 and 17 said the gospel reveals the righteousness of God. Verse 18 says the wrath of God is revealed too, and the same present tense verb, apokalyptetai, is used for both. Paul sets two revelations side by side, so the gospel cannot be understood as rescue until the danger it rescues from has been named. The passage that follows runs to 3:20 as one sustained indictment, and 1:18-32 is its first movement.

The paragraph is built like a descent. Verses 18 to 20 state the thesis: God's truth is plain and humanity pushes it down. Verses 21 to 23 trace the moral and intellectual fall, from refusing thanks to darkened thinking to idol making. Then comes a three part refrain. 'God gave them over' appears in verse 24, verse 26 and verse 28, and each time it is followed by a matching 'exchange' or failure of the previous section: the exchange of glory in verse 23 leads to impurity in verse 24, the exchange of truth for a lie in verse 25 leads to dishonorable passions in verses 26 and 27, and the refusal to acknowledge God in verse 28 leads to a debased mind. The sins get worse as the handing over deepens, and the passage ends with a long catalog of vices in verses 29 to 31 and a final verdict in verse 32.

Paul interrupts himself once. In verse 25, after speaking of worshiping the creature, he cannot help adding 'who is forever worthy of praise! Amen.' The doxology in the middle of an indictment is deliberate. The God being dishonored is still blessed, whatever people do.

Notice also the shift of pronouns. Verses 18 to 32 speak entirely of 'they,' a distant crowd. That is the trap Paul is setting. Chapter 2 opens with 'You,' and the reader who has been nodding along suddenly finds himself in the dock, Romans 2:1.
context.historical:
Paul probably wrote Romans from Corinth around AD 57, a few years after the Roman church's Jewish members had returned from the expulsion under the emperor Claudius that Acts 18:2 mentions. The church was a mix of Jewish and Gentile believers, and some of the tension in the letter grows from that mix. A Jewish reader hearing 1:18-32 would nod. It sounds like the standard Jewish account of the pagan world, and the Jewish Wisdom of Solomon, chapters 13 and 14, argues almost exactly this: that creation should have led people to its Maker, and that idolatry is the source of moral corruption.

The pagan world of the first century gave Paul plenty of material. Rome was full of temples, household gods and emperor worship, and the sexual and social vices he lists were open features of life in Greek and Roman cities, not secrets. Paul does not need to invent evidence. He expects his readers to know exactly what he means.

The language of exchange also reaches back into Israel's own history. When Israel made a calf at Horeb, Psalm 106:20 says 'They exchanged their Glory for the image of a grass-eating ox.' Jeremiah 2:11 asks whether a nation has ever changed its gods and answers that Israel has 'exchanged their Glory for useless idols.' Deuteronomy 4:16-18 forbids images in the likeness of man, beast, bird or creeping thing, the same categories Paul lists in verse 23. A listener steeped in the Scriptures would hear that Paul is describing the pagan world in the very terms Israel's own prophets used to describe Israel's failure. The Jew who agrees with chapter 1 has already agreed to a standard that will convict him in chapter 2.
context.canonical:
The passage reads the whole story of Genesis 1 to 11 in a single movement. The creatures of verse 23 are the creatures of Genesis 1:20-26, now worshiped instead of ruled. The exchange of truth for a lie is Genesis 3:4-5 again, with its promise that eating would make the pair 'like God.' The handing over to what the heart desires is the world before the flood, where the thoughts of the human heart were evil continually, Genesis 6:5.

God's handing over is a pattern the Old Testament already knows. Psalm 81:12 says 'So I gave them up to their stubborn hearts to follow their own devices.' Stephen says in Acts 7:42 that God 'turned away from them and gave them over to the worship of the host of heaven,' using the same Greek verb as Romans 1:24. The Old Testament prophets mock idols as lifeless things and add that 'Those who make them become like them,' Psalm 115:8. That is Romans 1 in a sentence: worship what is less than human and you become less than human.

Later in Romans the same themes return. The glory that humanity gave up is the glory they 'fall short of' in 3:23. The wrath revealed here is the wrath Christ turns away in 5:9. The knowledge of God through creation is the background to Paul's addresses in Acts 14:15-17 and Acts 17:22-31, where he speaks to pagans in just this way. And the catalog of verses 29 to 31 has parallels in the vice lists of 1 Corinthians 6:9-10, Galatians 5:19-21 and 2 Timothy 3:2-5, each of which sets the fallen life against life in the Spirit.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul writes to Christians in Rome who need to understand the gospel from the ground up, and he starts by proving what most of them already half believed: the world is not simply unfortunate, it is guilty. His strategy is to take the common Jewish critique of Gentile idolatry and press it to a larger conclusion. Everything he says about the Gentiles is true, and it will soon be shown to be true of everyone.

He also means the passage to explain how sin works, not only that it exists. Sin is not mainly a failure of information. The knowledge of God is 'plain to them' and the trouble is what they do with it: they suppress it, refuse to thank, and replace the Creator. The moral wreck of verses 24 to 31 is described as a consequence, not the cause. Idolatry comes first and disorder follows.

And he means to put the reader in an uncomfortable position. Verse 32 says those who do these things 'not only continue to do these things, but also approve of those who practice them.' The sin of approval catches the person who never does the worst deeds yet applauds them in others. Paul wants every self-satisfied observer to realize that the verdict has no exemptions, so that the free gift of chapter 3 can be received as a gift and not as a reward.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes. It tells us what idolatry looks like, how God judges it, and what a society that loses God looks like. It does not give a rule for the church to enforce on outsiders, and it does not give a checklist for deciding who is beyond hope. The very next words, Romans 2:1, forbid the reader from treating the passage as a weapon.

What carries forward is first a way of seeing. Every disorder in a person or a culture can be traced back to what is worshiped, so the church should look for idolatry beneath symptoms, including its own. Second, it carries forward a way of speaking. Paul preached to pagans with creation, rain and fruitful seasons as his first witness, Acts 14:17, and with the God who gives 'life and breath and all things,' Acts 17:25. Third, it carries a warning about drift. The handing over in this passage is gradual, so a person or a community can be slowly given over without any single dramatic step. The right response is not despair, since the same letter says 'where sin increased, grace increased all the more,' Romans 5:20, but repentance while there is time, Romans 2:4.

debates.question: What does 'God gave them over' mean?

views.label: Judicial abandonment
views.case: God withdraws His restraint and hands people to the consequences of their chosen course, and this is a real act of judgment. The phrase 'in the desires of their hearts,' verse 24, shows that He does not plant the desire but lets it have its way. Psalm 81:12 and Acts 7:42 use the same pattern. The historic Reformed and Lutheran reading takes the verb as active and judicial, with God remaining holy and not the author of sin, James 1:13.

views.label: Permission and natural consequence
views.case: Some stress that Paul describes sin working as its own punishment, like a fever that runs its course. On this view the handing over is closer to letting go than to pushing. It keeps God's hands clear of evil and fits the repeated 'exchange' language, which puts the human act first.

views.label: A step in a larger plan
views.case: Others note that the handing over is not final. Paul writes elsewhere of God handing over for a purpose, as with the incestuous man 'to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord,' 1 Corinthians 5:5. Romans 11:32 says God has consigned everyone to disobedience 'so that He may have mercy on everyone.'

debates.bearing: The judicial reading fits the grammar and the Old Testament pattern best, and the third view adds what the other two leave out: even this judgment serves the larger purpose of bringing people to the end of themselves. Sin as its own punishment is a mercy of a stern kind, since it exposes the need that the gospel answers.

debates.question: How should verses 26 and 27 be read today?

views.label: A judgment on same sex acts as contrary to creation
views.case: This has been the dominant reading across church history. Paul uses 'natural' (physis) and 'unnatural' (para physin) of acts that depart from the created pattern of man and woman in Genesis 1:27 and 2:24. Verse 27 explicitly describes men with men and women with women. On this reading Paul names the behavior as a sign of the creature taking the Creator's place.

views.label: A reference to exploitative or excessive practice in Greco-Roman culture
views.case: Some modern scholars argue Paul has in mind pederasty, cult prostitution or lust that exceeds natural limits, practices common in his world, and not committed same sex partnership as later understood. Critics reply that Paul's language is general, speaks of women as well as men, and refers to creation order, not to exploitation.

views.label: An illustration, not the point
views.case: A third emphasis holds that whatever one concludes, Paul is not ranking sins. The passage is about idolatry as the root, and verses 29 to 31 list envy, gossip, arrogance and disobedience to parents alongside sexual sin. The argument turns at 2:1, which condemns the judge who does the same things.

debates.bearing: Honest readers must note that the first view is the long standing reading of the text and that the others are attempts to qualify it, so each reader should weigh the case for himself. What all three share is Paul's own use of the passage: it humbles the reader, it does not license contempt. The wise application treats every sin in the catalog as evidence of one human condition, and every person as someone for whom Christ died, Romans 5:8.

debates.question: How much can creation tell us about God?

views.label: Enough to condemn, not to save
views.case: The traditional Protestant view holds that creation reveals God's power and nature so clearly, verse 20, that no one has an excuse, but not the gospel. Salvation requires the word of Christ, Romans 10:14-17. Verse 21 says people 'knew God' and still turned away, which is a knowledge that damns before it saves.

views.label: A real but corrupted knowledge
views.case: Calvin spoke of a sense of the divine in every person that sin distorts into idolatry. Paul's description of futile thinking and darkened hearts, verse 21, suits this view: the knowledge is present but twisted, so humanity makes gods in its own image.

views.label: A starting point for salvation without Christ
views.case: Some argue that creation might lead sincere seekers to saving faith without hearing the gospel. Others reply that Paul sees no one responding rightly: 'there is no one who seeks God,' Romans 3:11, and he sends missionaries in Romans 10:14-15 because hearing is how faith comes.

debates.bearing: The text keeps its weight on the guilt of the knower. Paul does not say here what God does with those who have never heard, and he does not give a basis for assuming that any are saved without Christ. What he insists on is that no one will be able to say they had no light.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's verbs in verse 18 carry more than the English shows. The wrath is 'being revealed,' apokalyptetai, the very verb used in verse 17 for the righteousness of God. Both revelations are happening now, not only at the last day. The people described 'suppress' the truth, katechontes, from katecho, a verb that means to hold something down or hold it back. The picture is of someone sitting on a spring: the truth keeps pushing up and has to be held under by constant effort. Paul's word for 'wickedness,' adikia, is the opposite of the righteousness, dikaiosyne, he just announced. And 'without excuse,' verse 20, is anapologetous, literally 'without a defense speech.' It is a courtroom word, and it begins the long trial that will end with every mouth stopped at 3:19.

Verse 20 plays with sight. The 'invisible qualities,' ta aorata, are 'clearly seen,' kathoratai, and 'understood,' nooumena. The invisible is seen through the mind looking at what has been made. The verb tenses say this has been true 'since the creation of the world,' and it is still true.

In verse 21 the thinking that becomes 'futile' comes from mataios, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for worthless idols and empty things. The echo is deliberate, and it matches Jeremiah 2:5, where Israel followed worthless things and became worthless themselves. Those who worship nothing become nothing. 'Darkened' and 'foolish' hearts match the word for 'senseless' in verse 31, so the passage closes on the same lack of understanding with which the fall began.

Three different verbs for 'exchange' mark the slide. In verse 23 humanity exchanged the glory of God for images, the same verb family Psalm 106:20 uses of the calf. In verse 25 they exchanged the truth for 'the lie,' with the article, which many take to mean the great lie that a creature can be God. Verse 26 speaks of exchanging natural relations for unnatural ones. In verses 26 and 27 the term 'natural' is physis, the way things are made, and 'unnatural' is para physin, 'against nature.' Paul applies the same moral vocabulary to idolatry and to disordered desire, so he is thinking of both as departures from a created order.

Finally, verse 28 turns on a pun that English loses. 'They did not see fit' translates edokimasan, and God 'gave them up to a depraved mind,' adokimos nous, a mind that has failed the test. They tested God and rejected Him, and God handed them a mind that cannot test anything. The catalog that follows includes 'God-haters,' theostygeis, a word that can also mean 'hated by God,' and 'they invent new forms of evil,' epheuretas kakon, 'inventors of evil.' Verse 32 ends on syneudokousin, 'they approve,' literally to take delight together. The final sin is a kind of fellowship in evil.

typology.type: Eden: the lie that the creature may be like God, Genesis 3:4-5
typology.fulfillment: The serpent's promise that eating would make the pair 'like God' is the pattern Paul sees in verse 25, the truth exchanged for the lie that creatures can take God's place. Adam stands as the head of a humanity that repeats his choice, which Paul develops in Romans 5:12-21. In Christ the pattern is reversed. He is the one 'existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped,' Philippians 2:6, and He receives glory by obedience. The type falls short in one respect: Adam's exchange was a single act in a garden, while the idolatry of Romans 1 is the habit of the whole race.

typology.type: The golden calf at Horeb, Psalm 106:19-20
typology.fulfillment: Israel exchanged its Glory for the image of a grass eating ox, and Paul takes that exchange as the shape of all idolatry. The calf was supposedly a way to worship the LORD, Exodus 32:4-5, which shows how near the exchange can come to religion. What the calf could not do, Christ does. He is 'the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature,' Hebrews 1:3, the true image that does not replace the Creator but reveals Him. The type is limited because the calf was a rival image; Christ is the image God Himself gave.

Humans were made to image the invisible God, and Romans 1 shows the image turned upside down: instead of reflecting God, they carve gods in the likeness of man and beast. Paul calls Christ 'the image of the invisible God,' Colossians 1:15, and says believers are being 'transformed into His image with intensifying glory,' 2 Corinthians 3:18. The image lost is renewed in the new self, 'created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness,' Ephesians 4:24. The correspondence is not a one to one picture of Christ in Genesis, but the NT teaches the restoring of the image as the goal of salvation.

typology.type: Handing over: Israel in judgment and Christ delivered up
typology.fulfillment: God handed Israel to its idols, Acts 7:42, and handed the nations to their desires, Romans 1:24, 26, 28. The same verb returns at the cross: God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32, and Jesus 'was delivered over to death for our trespasses,' Romans 4:25. The sinner is given over to sin's consequences, and the Son is given over so that the consequences fall on Him. The correspondence is in the verb, and the escalation is that the judicial act of chapter 1 becomes the saving act of chapter 8.

study.christ:
The verb that organizes this passage is the verb that organizes the gospel. God 'gave them over,' paredoken, three times in Romans 1. Paul uses the same verb of Christ: God 'gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32, and He 'was delivered over to death for our trespasses,' Romans 4:25. In chapter 1 the Father hands sinners to their sin. At the cross He hands His Son into the judgment sinners deserve. The mercy of Calvary is the handing over of Romans 1 turned around, so that those who were abandoned might be received.

Christ is also the answer to each of the great exchanges. Where humanity suppressed the truth, Jesus says 'I am the way and the truth and the life,' John 14:6. Where humanity exchanged the glory of God for images, He is 'the radiance of God's glory,' Hebrews 1:3, 'the image of the invisible God,' Colossians 1:15, and John 1:14 says 'we have seen His glory.' Where humanity refused to give thanks, the Son 'gave thanks' and broke the bread, Luke 22:19, and His people are told to give thanks in everything, 1 Thessalonians 5:18. And the wrath revealed from heaven in verse 18 is met at the place Paul describes a few verses later: God presented Him as 'the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood,' Romans 3:25. Having been justified, 'saved from wrath through Him,' Romans 5:9.

Even the final sin of verse 32 has its answer. The people described not only sin but approve those who do. In Christ's own story the opposite happened. Pilate's crowd, Luke 23:18-23, approved the wrong man, and Jesus prayed 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,' Luke 23:34. The one who died for approvers of evil is the One who can reverse a debased mind. Paul says in Romans 12:2 that believers are 'transformed by the renewing of your mind,' which meets the adokimos nous of 1:28 with a mind that can test and approve the will of God, using the same family of words.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Romans 1 does not name Christ, and not every detail is a picture of Him. The links rest on Paul's own repeated words, paredoken, doxa and eikon, and on the way the argument of chapters 1 to 8 moves from wrath to 'no condemnation,' Romans 8:1. The darkness of the first chapter is there so that the cross can be seen for what it is.
study.god:
The God of this passage is the Creator who makes Himself known. Verses 19 and 20 insist that God 'has made it plain' and that His power and divine nature are visible in His works. Nothing here says God is hiding. The problem is not on the side of the revealer. This is the God of Psalm 19:1, whose heavens declare His glory, and who gives rain and fruitful seasons to people who do not thank Him, Acts 14:17.

He is the God whose wrath is real. Paul does not soften it, and he does not treat it as a mood. It is revealed 'against all the godlessness and wickedness of men,' verse 18, as the settled response of a holy God to evil. Wrath is not the opposite of love in Scripture; it is what love looks like when it meets what destroys the beloved. A God who did not mind idolatry, cruelty and deceit would not be good. Yet the Bible also says that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, Ezekiel 18:23, and that His kindness 'leads you to repentance,' Romans 2:4. These do not contradict each other. Patience is the form wrath takes while mercy still holds the door.

He is a God who judges by letting sin ripen. The handing over is not a lack of power. It shows that God can punish sin by giving it exactly what it wants, so that the pursuit of self leads to emptiness. That is a solemn thing, and Paul wants it felt. It also shows that God is not the author of the evil, since each time the people's own desire and exchange is named first.

He is the God who is worthy of worship whatever people do. The doxology of verse 25, 'who is forever worthy of praise! Amen,' declares that His glory is not reduced when it is exchanged. What is lost by sinners is theirs to lose, and His praise does not depend on them. The same apostle finishes the great argument of Romans with 'To Him be the glory forever! Amen,' Romans 11:36.

Finally, He is the God of jealous love. The passage describes God leaving people to what they chose, and in the logic of Scripture that is the most terrible thing God can do. His own people knew the other possibility, for the LORD says in Hosea 11:8, 'How could I give you up, O Ephraim?' The God who hands people over in Romans 1 is the God who hands over His own Son in Romans 8. For worship this means two things at once: reverence before a holy Judge, and gratitude that the Judge Himself has borne the sentence.

crossReferences.note: The two verses just before. The gospel reveals God's righteousness, and in verse 18 the wrath of God is revealed in the same present tense. Paul states the cure before he describes the disease, so the reader knows the darkness is not the last word.
The heavens declare God's glory, and their voice goes out to all the earth. Paul takes this as the ground of verse 20: creation speaks to everyone, so everyone is accountable for what it says.

God asks whether any nation has ever exchanged its gods, and charges Israel with exchanging its Glory for useless idols. Paul's word 'exchanged' in verse 23 comes from this prophetic accusation, so the Jewish reader hears Israel's own indictment applied to the nations.

At Horeb Israel exchanged its Glory for the image of an ox. Paul turns this event into the pattern for all humanity: a people who knew God's glory most closely still preferred an image they could hold.

The makers of idols become like them, mouths that cannot speak, eyes that cannot see. This is the same law of exchange seen from the other side: worship what is less than human and you become less than human, which is the debased mind of Romans 1:28.

God says He gave His people up to their stubborn hearts to follow their own devices. This is the Old Testament form of the handing over in Romans 1:24, 26 and 28, and it shows that Paul is describing a known way God judges, not an unusual new doctrine.

Stephen says God turned away and gave the people over to the worship of the host of heaven. The Greek verb is the one Paul uses three times in Romans 1. Idolatry followed by judicial abandonment is a pattern in Israel's history, not only in the Gentile world.

Paul and Barnabas tell a pagan crowd to turn from worthless things to the living God who made all things and gave rain and fruitful seasons as His testimony. It is Romans 1:19-20 as preaching, and it shows how creation was the opening of the conversation with Gentiles.

At Athens Paul argues that if we are God's offspring we should not think the Divine Being is like gold or stone. He adds that God overlooked the ignorance of earlier times and now commands repentance. It is the same charge as Romans 1:23, joined to a call to turn.

Christ died for us while we were still sinners, and so we are saved from wrath through Him. The wrath revealed in 1:18 is not simply endured by sinners. It is borne by another, which is why the passage that describes humanity at its worst can sit inside a letter about the love of God.

God did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all. The verb 'gave up' is the same one used of God handing sinners over in Romans 1:24, 26 and 28, so the cross is set against the judgment of the first chapter.

Believers are to be transformed by the renewing of the mind so that they can test and approve what God's will is. This answers the debased mind of 1:28, where people failed to test and approve God. The remedy is a mind renewed in the same terms in which the disease was described.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a world that is very good and a humanity that bears God's image, Genesis 1:26-31. The first human choice is described by Paul as an exchange: the truth of God for a lie. Romans 1:18-32 is the New Testament's most compact account of what happens after that, and it answers a question every reader eventually asks. If God is good and has made Himself known, why is the world so broken? The answer is not that God is absent or hidden. It is that people turned from a God they could see.

The story that follows in Genesis proves the point. Cain's murder, Genesis 4:8, the corruption before the flood, Genesis 6:5, and the pride of Babel, Genesis 11:4, all fit the pattern of verses 21 to 32: the refusal of thanks, the darkened heart, the invention of new evil. Then God calls Abraham so that all families of the earth will be blessed, Genesis 12:3, and Israel is given the law and the tabernacle, with the very command against images that Paul alludes to here. Yet Israel exchanges its Glory for a calf, and the prophets say Israel is no better than the nations, Jeremiah 2:11 and Ezekiel 16. Paul's point, once chapter 2 is reached, is that Israel is under the same verdict.

This is the darkness the gospel enters. When Jesus comes, He is 'the true Light who gives light to every man,' John 1:9, in a world where people loved darkness, John 3:19. The cross answers the exchange. God gives up His Son so that sinners given over might be brought back, and Pentecost begins to reverse the confusion and idolatry of the nations by gathering people from every tongue, Acts 2:5-11.

The new creation answers Romans 1 point by point. In the new Jerusalem there is no temple of stone or image, 'for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. Those who were given over to idols are replaced by those who worship the Creator, Revelation 4:11, and the catalog of vices of verses 29 to 31 finds an echo in the vices excluded from the city, Revelation 21:8 and 22:15. The image of God, defaced in Genesis 3 and exchanged for lies in Romans 1, is restored when 'they will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads,' Revelation 22:4. Creation itself waits for that day, Romans 8:19-21. The question 'why is the world like this?' is answered here, and the one that follows, 'what will God do about it?', is answered by everything that comes after.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say people are without excuse before God?

options.text: Because God's eternal power and divine nature are clearly seen in creation, yet they suppress that truth.
options.note: Verses 19 and 20 say God's qualities are plain in creation, leaving people without excuse.

options.text: Because they never had any way of knowing God at all.
options.note: The opposite is true: what may be known of God is plain to them, which is why they are without excuse.

options.text: Because they broke the law of Moses given to Israel.
options.note: Law-breaking does condemn, but Paul's argument here concerns the witness of creation to all people; he takes up the law later.

options.text: Because they failed to attend proper worship.
options.note: The issue is suppressing the truth about God known through creation, not neglecting religious rituals.

quiz.q: What is the root exchange Paul describes at the heart of human sin?

options.text: They exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of created things.
options.note: Verse 23 names idolatry, trading God's glory for images, as the fundamental exchange.

options.text: They exchanged wealth for poverty by unwise living.
options.note: The exchange Paul names is theological, God's glory for idols, not a financial one.

options.text: They exchanged the truth of God for a lie in their thinking.
options.note: This is genuinely part of it, verse 25, and flows from the idolatry, though the root exchange named in verse 23 is trading God's glory for images.

options.text: They exchanged old traditions for new customs.
options.note: The real exchange is the glory of God for images, an act of idolatry, not mere cultural change.

quiz.q: What does the repeated phrase God gave them over mean?

options.text: God, in judgment, handed rebels over to the desires they chose, so that sin became its own punishment.
options.note: The threefold handing over is a present, judicial expression of God's wrath.

options.text: God withdrew His restraint and let their chosen sin run its course.
options.note: Very close: this captures the judicial abandonment, though Paul's verb stresses an active handing over, not mere withdrawal.

options.text: God simply stood by with no involvement at all.
options.note: The handing over is an active, judicial act, not divine absence or indifference.

options.text: God forced people to sin against their will.
options.note: God gave them over to desires they already had; He is not the author of their sin.

quiz.q: How does this passage function within Paul's larger argument in Romans?

options.text: It exposes the universal human problem of sin and wrath that the gospel's righteousness answers.
options.note: Paul is proving the need for the gospel by showing all are under wrath.

options.text: It shows that Gentile idolaters stand under God's judgment, beginning the case that all are guilty.
options.note: Right as far as it goes: this is the first stage, but Paul extends the indictment to the respectable and to Israel in the chapters that follow.

options.text: It offers a program of moral self-improvement.
options.note: The passage diagnoses the problem; the remedy is the righteousness of God by faith, not self-improvement.

options.text: It denies that God cares about human behavior.
options.note: The revealing of wrath shows God cares deeply about evil and its ruin.

quiz.q: What is true of those who practice the sins Paul catalogs in verses 29 to 32?

options.text: They know God's righteous decree that such things deserve death, yet continue and even approve of others who do them.
options.note: Verse 32 stresses their knowledge of the verdict and their approval of evil.

options.text: They know such things are wrong but do them anyway in weakness.
options.note: They do know the decree, but Paul says more: they not only continue but openly approve of others who practice such things.

options.text: They act in complete ignorance of any moral standard.
options.note: Paul says they know God's righteous decree, so it is not sheer ignorance.

options.text: They are excused because everyone behaves this way.
options.note: Universality does not excuse; Paul says they are worthy of death and without excuse.

questions: Paul says the truth about God is plain in creation, yet people suppress it. Where do you see this suppression at work today, and where might you be tempted to it yourself?
The root of sin here is exchanging the glory of God for lesser things. What functional idols compete for the worship your heart owes to God alone?
God's wrath is revealed partly by giving people over to the desires they insist on. How does this sober picture of sin becoming its own punishment change the way you view your own struggles with sin?
This passage insists that no one is without excuse. How does facing the depth of the human problem make the righteousness of God in the gospel more precious to you?
Verse 32 warns not only against doing evil but approving those who do it. Where are you tempted to applaud or excuse what God calls wrong, and how should the gospel reshape that?
Christ bore the wrath this passage describes so that idolaters might be restored to God's glory. How does that move you to worship the Creator who is forever worthy of praise?

translationNotes.note: Who suppress the truth by their wickedness renders a verb meaning to hold down or restrain; the picture is of actively pressing the truth about God out of sight, not passively lacking it.

God gave them over translates a strong verb meaning to hand over or deliver up. Repeated in verses 26 and 28, it describes a judicial act of God in which He withdraws restraint and delivers sinners to their chosen desires.

A depraved mind renders a word meaning failing the test, unfit, or disqualified. There is a deliberate play: because they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to an unfit mind, a mind that can no longer judge rightly.
